questions.question: Why didn't physicians trust the ambient scribe's draft notes?
questions.answer: Physicians were skeptical of the ambient scribe's draft notes because medication dosage errors were present in 3 of 5 sessions during the v0.1 stage. [1] Even after errors dropped in v0.2, physicians still read every line because they didn't feel a difference in the experience. [1] Physicians also said that medication dosage errors were disqualifying for direct sign-off without review. [2]

sources.title: The Longitudinal Physician — Ambient Scribe Journey (v0.1 to Post-GA)
sources.excerpt:
v0.1 (Feb 2025) — Skeptical, reads every generated line; medication dosage errors present in 3 of 5 sessions reinforce that caution.
v0.2 (Sep 2025) — Errors drop, but reading behavior doesn't — still reads every line despite the accuracy gain. A frustration plateau: "why doesn't this feel any different?"
GA Candidate (Jan 2026) — Per-line confidence highlighting introduces the first behavior change: begins skimming high-confidence lines for the first time. Relief, tempered by sound-alike medication names still being a known, monitored gap.
sources.contextBefore: Follows the longitudinal physician persona (composite of participant P09) across all four ambient-scribe touchpoints she's been part of over the past year.
sources.contextAfter: Post-GA (Feb 2026) — The dedicated medication-safety flag reads as more actionable than generic confidence highlighting — but only if unflagged lines don't get over-trusted as a result. Session lock during dictation remains a trust risk entirely unrelated to transcription quality — a "the tool ate my work" scare that isn't actually true.

sources.title: Clinician Experience & Documentation Burden
sources.excerpt: Documentation burden is real and quantifiable, not just anecdotal. The September baseline found documentation burden is physicians' #1 self-selected burnout driver (52%, ahead of patient volume at 31%), with 64% doing regular after-hours "pajama time" charting (avg. 1.2 hrs/day). This is now the official pre-AI baseline for measuring Compass AI's impact at 6 and 12 months post-GA. Caveat: the September survey mentioned the AI initiative explicitly in its framing, while the February survey didn't — any comparison between the two datasets needs to account for that framing difference, not treat them as a clean before/after.
sources.contextBefore: The top volunteered concern was not accuracy or privacy — it was voice. questions.question: What did coders think of the AI billing code suggestions?
questions.answer:
Senior coders were concerned that AI suggesting codes could be seen as steering toward upcoding if not carefully positioned. They wanted explicit documentation that the human coder made the final call, not the AI, in case of an audit. [1][2]

In 14 of 20 test scenarios, the AI suggestions matched the coder's own independent choice. Mismatches were mostly about specificity level (e.g., unspecified vs. specified diagnosis) rather than category-level. [2]

sources.title: HIM: Coding, Billing & Release of Information
sources.excerpt: AI-assisted coding suggestions (usability test) surfaced the same underlying concern in a different shape : the senior coder's objection wasn't accuracy (14/20 suggestions matched independent human judgment) but audit posture — she wanted it explicit in the UI and audit log that the human coder made the final call, to avoid the suggestion looking like it steered toward upcoding. This is the same "show your work" / attribution-of-decision pattern seen in prior authorization testing (see [prior-authorization.md](prior-authorization.md)).
sources.contextBefore: …never auto-redact-and-release. This session also surfaced a standalone platform gap — there's no structured way to flag a note as Part 2-protected in the EHR — that recurred again independently in the October behavioral health research (see [scope-boundaries-and-workflow-fit.md](scope-boundaries-and-workflow-fit.md)), making it a two-source-confirmed gap worth fixing regardless of any AI plans.
sources.contextAfter: Recommendation: any AI feature touching this department needs an explicit, audit-log-visible human-decision boundary as a baseline requirement, not a design nicety — this shows up whether the task is redaction, coding, or (per the prior-auth findings) authorization drafting.

questions.question: What did the prior auth usability tests find?
questions.answer:
The v1 usability test found that in 2 of 4 cases, the AI draft cited outdated diagnosis codes. Participants said this would likely cause a payer denial if submitted. [1] The supervisor said nurses would still need to read every AI-drafted justification in full before submission because a wrongly submitted prior auth can delay patient care. [1]

The v2 follow-up test found that the outdated diagnosis code issue did not recur in any of the 4 test cases. [2] Inline source citations were well-received and used actively — 3 of 4 participants clicked into at least one citation to verify before accepting. [2]

sources.title: Ambient AI Scribe
sources.excerpt:
The ambient AI scribe has moved from a formative concept (v0.1, Feb 2025) through iteration (v0.2, Sep 2025) to a GA release candidate (Jan 2026), with 3 of the original 5 physician participants retained across all three rounds for longitudinal comparison.
PHI handling: The critical draft-retention/audit gap found in v0.1 was fixed by v0.2 and has remained stable through the GA candidate — drafts auto-expire after 10 minutes of inactivity and the behavior is documented for Compliance. No PHI-handling issues have recurred since.
sources.contextAfter: Accuracy: Medication dosage errors dropped from 3/5 sessions (v0.1) to 1/5 (v0.2), driven by fixing outright garbling; the remaining error class is specifically sound-alike medication names, which is now a tracked, monitored issue rather than a blocker.

questions.question: How did physicians react to the medication flag concept?
questions.answer:
Five out of six participants in a concept test correctly identified the medication-specific flag as different from the generic low-confidence underline. [1]

Two participants said the badge's specificity made them more likely to treat unflagged medication lines as automatically correct. [1]

A distinct sound-alike-medication flag outperforms generic confidence highlighting for this specific error class. [2]

sources.title: Usability Test — Ambient Scribe Sound-Alike Medication Flag Concept
sources.excerpt:
[HIGH] (flag recognized correctly) 5 of 6 participants correctly identified the medication-specific flag (a distinct amber pill-shaped badge, vs. the generic low-confidence underline) as "different from the usual low-confidence thing" within the first two encounters, without being told the distinction existed.
[MEDIUM] (over-trust risk) 2 participants said the badge's specificity made them more likely to treat unflagged medication lines as automatically correct — the opposite of the intended effect, and worth watching as adoption scales.

sources.title: Ambient Scribe — Post-GA Refinements
sources.excerpt: A distinct sound-alike-medication flag outperforms generic confidence highlighting for this specific error class. The GA-candidate round treated sound-alike medication errors as an ongoing monitoring item, relying on the general confidence-highlighted variant to surface them. A concept test of a dedicated, visually distinct flag found 5 of 6 participants correctly recognized it as categorically different from generic low confidence — but also surfaced a new risk: 2 of 6 participants said the flag's specificity made them trust unflagged medication lines more than they should. Any rollout needs to actively counter that over-trust framing, not just ship the flag.

sources.title: AI-Assisted Prior Authorization
sources.excerpt:
AI-drafted prior authorization justifications were tested in two rounds (v1, Apr 2025; v2, Nov 2025) with the same utilization review nurse supervisor across both, which mattered for tracking whether fixes actually landed.
v1 surfaced a correctness bug (citing outdated diagnosis codes) serious enough that participants said it would likely cause payer denials — not a UX problem, a data-freshness/model fix. It also surfaced a durable requirement: nurses want inline citations to the specific chart text behind each suggestion ("show your work"), not just a black-box draft.
sources.contextAfter: v2 , after both fixes landed, confirmed the outdated-code issue did not recur and that the citation feature is actively used (3 of 4 participants checked at least one citation before accepting) rather than being ignored as friction.

questions.question: How much drafting time did the AI save on prior auth cases?

Participants estimated the AI cut initial drafting time from ~15 minutes to ~5 minutes per straightforward case when the citation was correct [1].

This was confirmed in v2 testing, with drafting time confirmed at ~5 minutes vs. ~15 minutes manual for straightforward cases [2][3].

questions.question: Why did new admins hesitate at the Connect calendar step?
questions.answer:
New admins hesitated at step 3 ("Connect calendar") because the wording implied the step was optional, when it's actually required for later functionality. [1][2][3][4]

Two out of three participants in the first three usability sessions attempted to skip step 3 outright, assuming it was optional. [2] In session 1, the participant paused for 15 seconds at step 3, saying "wait, do I have to do this?" before proceeding. [4]

sources.title: Onboarding flow — setup step confusion
sources.excerpt:
New admins hesitate at, or attempt to skip, step 3 of the onboarding wizard ("Connect calendar") because its wording implies the step is optional, when it's actually required for later functionality. This is the largest single source of friction in first-time setup.
A separate, related hesitation sits at step 4 ("Invite your team"): admins aren't sure whether invites send immediately or only when the wizard is submitted.
